name: OKLCH Colour Picker
summary: Picks in perceptual space, so dragging lightness does not shift apparent hue. Each slider previews its own axis, and the sRGB gamut edge is detected by painting the colour and reading the pixel back.

attempts.prompt: Build a colour picker using OKLCH.
attempts.problem: Three range inputs with plain grey tracks and a swatch. Nothing previewed what dragging would do, so choosing a colour meant dragging blindly and watching the result. Out-of-gamut values were accepted silently: pushing chroma past what sRGB can show produced a swatch that stopped changing while the number kept climbing, with no indication that the display had run out.

attempts.prompt: Add gradient previews behind each slider and warn when out of gamut.
attempts.problem: The ramps were computed once at load, so they never updated as the other two axes moved — the hue ramp still showed hues at the original lightness after lightness had changed. The gamut warning used a hand-written sRGB conversion that disagreed with the browser's own rendering at the edges, so it warned on colours that displayed fine and missed ones that clipped.

finalPrompt:
Build an OKLCH colour picker in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies.

Three range inputs for lightness, chroma and hue, a large swatch, and the resulting oklch() string with a copy button.

Each slider's track must be a gradient previewing the axis it controls, generated from the current values of the other two, and regenerated on every change. A hue ramp drawn at the wrong lightness is worse than no ramp, because it promises a colour the slider will not produce. Build the ramps as linear-gradient strings of nine oklch() stops and set them as a custom property on the input, styling ::-webkit-slider-runnable-track and ::-moz-range-track from it.

Detect the sRGB gamut edge by measurement, not by arithmetic. Paint the requested colour into a 1x1 canvas, read the pixel back, and treat a channel pinned at 0 or 255 with meaningful chroma as out of gamut. A hand-written conversion will disagree with the browser at exactly the edges that matter; asking the browser what it actually painted cannot.

When out of gamut, say so plainly and state that the swatch is showing the nearest displayable colour.

Show lightness to one decimal with a percent sign, chroma to three decimals, and hue as a whole number of degrees, all tabular-nums so the figures do not jump while dragging.

Style the thumb and track explicitly for both WebKit and Firefox — a range input left at browser defaults is the clearest sign a picker was assembled rather than built.

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties for the chrome: var(--bg), var(--raised), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent). The picked colour itself is of course arbitrary and lives in a custom property set by script.
why:
Two lessons, and the second is the transferable one.

The first is that a preview which does not track the other axes is actively misleading. Saying a hue ramp drawn at the wrong lightness is worse than no ramp explains the why, and the why is what stopped the model computing the ramps once at load.

The second: prefer measurement to reimplementation. The gamut question has an exact answer already available — paint it and look — and any hand-rolled conversion will disagree with the renderer precisely at the boundary being tested. Whenever a component needs to know what the browser will do, the cheapest correct answer is usually to let the browser do it and inspect the result. That instruction generalises well beyond colour.
